melbfoot

Purpose

melbfoot helps people who plan around foot traffic in central Melbourne, such as café owners and event planners, answer a practical question: when and where are the most people walking past, and how much has foot traffic changed since 2025?

The package contains the data, two helper functions and a Shiny app:

  • ped_hourly: average pedestrians per hour for each sensor, year and type of day (weekday or weekend).
  • ped_sensors: where each sensor is.
  • hourly_profile(): pulls out the typical-day pattern for chosen sensors and years.
  • change_index(): compares each year’s average daily traffic with a baseline year (the earliest year in the data, 2025, by default).
  • launch_app(): opens the Shiny app.

Data

The data come from the City of Melbourne Pedestrian Counting System (counts per hour) and its Sensor Locations dataset, published on the City of Melbourne Open Data Portal. The Sensor Locations dataset is licensed CC BY 4.0. The portal page for the counts dataset does not state a licence, so the City of Melbourne is credited as the source throughout.

The raw hourly counts are large, so the package includes a summarised version: average pedestrians per hour, by sensor, year and day type. The portal data start in November 2024 and run to early November 2026, so to make years comparable the package keeps only 1 January to 2 November in 2025 and 2026. The script data-raw/ped_data.R downloads the raw files and builds the packaged data, so the process can be reproduced.

Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-inayat-gill")

Launch the app 

library(melbfoot)
launch_app()

In the app, choose up to three sensor locations, pick the years to compare and choose weekday or weekend. The first tab shows the typical hour-by-hour pattern and the busiest hour for each sensor. The second tab shows how each year’s daily traffic compares with 2025. The third tab explains the fields and what to keep in mind when reading the charts. A step-by-step guide is in the vignette: vignette("getting-started", package = "melbfoot").

Example 

library(melbfoot)

# Typical weekday in the latest year for the sensor with the most data
busiest <- ped_hourly$location_id[which.max(ped_hourly$n_days)]
hourly_profile(sensors = busiest, years = max(ped_hourly$year), day = "Weekday")

# How has daily traffic at the same sensor changed since 2025?
change_index(sensors = busiest)

Full documentation, including a getting-started guide and the function reference, is on the package website: https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-inayat-gill/
